# Geopolitical Consumer Activism in a Global Brand System
## "One Conduct Standard, Local Facts, No Borrowed Sides"

---

## 1. The core diagnostic

Global brands caught in geopolitical boycotts fail in seven recognisable ways, and all seven are versions of the same mistake: treating the crisis as a **communications problem about a brand** when it is in fact a **solvency, contractual and legal problem inside a multi-owner franchise system, in which the entity being punished is almost never the entity being blamed.**

**A logo is not a legal entity. A boycott is not a market.** Your unit of exposure is *this store, owned by this franchisee, under this agreement, employing these nationals, targeted by this actor, for this specific alleged act.* In most international F&B systems, the boycotted outlet is owned by a local family or a listed local operator, staffed almost entirely by local citizens, sourcing a majority of inputs locally, and remitting a single-digit royalty to the parent. The boycott transfers almost all of its economic damage to the local economy it intends to defend. That asymmetry is the central fact of the situation — and it is worthless to you unless it was **audited and published before the crisis started.**

**There is no local audience.** Any statement made in Jakarta is screenshotted in Tel Aviv within the hour, and vice versa. Geo-fenced messaging, "regionally sensitive" wording and quiet local reassurance are not tactics; they are the single most reliable way to convert a one-region problem into a two-region problem plus a credibility problem. Two contradictory statements do not cancel out. They compound, and the compound is *"they will say anything."*

**You are being asked to take a position on something you did not do, and the four cases require opposite responses.** Boycott triggers divide into: (a) something the company actually did; (b) something a franchisee, bottler, licensee or employee did independently; (c) something the company's *home state* did; (d) something falsely attributed. Apologising for (d) rewards fabrication and invites more. Correcting facts in (a) is stonewalling. Treating (b) as a brand act destroys the franchise model; treating it as "nothing to do with us" destroys the brand promise. (c) is not answerable by communications at all — only by pre-existing, verifiable local rootedness. **Most crisis teams pick one posture and apply it to all four.**

**You have put sentiment on the dashboard, so you now manage sentiment.** Share of voice, sentiment score and follower delta measure the loudest cohort, are trivially brigaded by coordinated campaigns and by bots on both sides, and correlate weakly with purchase. Meanwhile the metric that actually determines whether the damage is permanent — *whether a local substitute achieved taste-parity and shelf-parity during the window* — is on nobody's slide. **You will win the sentiment recovery and lose the category.**

**Discounting into a values boycott is the classic own-goal.** People boycotting on identity grounds are not price-sensitive on that axis. Promotion subsidises the loyalists who never left, trains the trade to wait for the next cut, permanently damages price architecture, and reads as desperation to the very audience you are trying to reach. You have paid margin to accelerate your own commoditisation.

**Franchisee demands for public statements are almost always mispriced requests for money.** A partner whose same-store sales are down 40% and who is three months from breaching a bank covenant asks for the thing he thinks you can give: a statement. He does not primarily want prose. He wants royalty relief, marketing-fund forbearance, rent renegotiation support, capex deferral and a solvency bridge. Answering the literal request generates a statement that damages another region and does not save him. **Vague solidarity is more damaging than a bounded, written, financial instrument.**

**"Just comply locally" is frequently illegal.** US anti-boycott rules (EAR Part 760; IRC §999) prohibit US persons and, in defined circumstances, their controlled foreign subsidiaries from complying with or furnishing information in support of unsanctioned foreign boycotts, and require *reporting* of boycott requests received. Some 35+ US states restrict contracting with entities that boycott particular states. Several European jurisdictions have prosecuted boycott advocacy on nationality grounds (France, art. 24 of the 1881 law; constrained but not eliminated by *Baldassi v. France*, ECtHR 2020). Sanctions regimes cut across all of it. Simultaneously, CSRD/CSDDD-style human-rights due-diligence obligations mean **"we are apolitical" is no longer available as a legal posture on human-rights conduct** — only on geopolitical alignment. The framework must distinguish those two things or it will be incoherent in both directions.

---

## 2. The resolution

**Separate *conduct* from *alignment*. They have been fused, and that fusion is the whole problem.**

- **Conduct** — how the company and its system behave: sourcing, employment, non-discrimination, safety, human-rights due diligence, sanctions compliance, humanitarian response, political-donation transparency. This is **global, uniform, published, auditable and genuinely non-negotiable**. It is the only legitimate subject of a corporate position.
- **Alignment** — endorsement of a state, party, movement or side in an armed or political conflict. This is **never adopted, in any market, in any language, by any entity in the system**, and that refusal is published *in peacetime* as a standing policy, not improvised as an evasion mid-crisis.

**The one-sentence answer: conduct is global, facts are local, positions are held only on our own actions — and any sentence we cannot publish in every market on the same day is not published in any of them.**

---

## 3. Decompose "boycott" into seven distinct phenomena

The word hides seven mechanics with different reversibility. The critical column is the last one: **who has the authority to end it, and what would they accept.**

| # | Phenomenon | Mechanism | Reversibility | Who can end it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Organised campaign** | Named organisers, explicit demands, target lists | High — it is a negotiation | The organisers. Ask: *would we grant this demand if anyone else asked?* |
| 2 | **State-adjacent boycott** | Ministry guidance, municipal delisting, parliamentary canteen bans, procurement exclusion | Medium — political cycle-bound | Government. Managed by government-affairs, not marketing |
| 3 | **Quasi-regulatory / religious ruling** | Certification-body rulings, fatwas, standards councils | Low-medium; often needs a formal countervailing process | The issuing body, via its own procedure |
| 4 | **Channel / retailer delisting** | Buyers pre-emptively de-range to avoid store-level protest | High, but commercially decisive | Category buyers. One delisting outweighs 100k hostile posts |
| 5 | **Institutional divestment** | Pension funds, universities, sovereign funds | Slow both ways | Investment committees; IR-owned |
| 6 | **Diffuse consumer sentiment** | No organiser, no demand, no off-switch | Decays on a half-life; unnegotiable | **Nobody.** Manage as weather, not as a negotiation |
| 7 | **Counter-boycott ("buycott")** | Opposing side rewards perceived alignment | Volatile; creates a trap | Nobody — and courting it converts you into a permanent political symbol |

**Rule:** categories 1–5 have counterparties and therefore admit strategy. Category 6 admits only operational endurance. Category 7 is the most dangerous, because accepting its revenue looks like free upside and is in fact the purchase of a permanent side.

---

## 4. Trigger tiers (governs by what happened, not by which region is angry)

| Tier | Trigger | Correct response | Prohibited response |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A — We did it** | Company action, policy, donation, contract, ad | Investigate fast, state findings, **change the thing if it was wrong**, publish the change globally | Facts-only defence; "misunderstanding" framing |
| **B — A system partner did it** | Franchisee donation, licensee statement, bottler action, employee post

run.userPrompt:
In 2025-2026, waves of geopolitically motivated consumer boycotts, amplified by social media and national sentiment, have hit global consumer brands unevenly across regions. A global food-and-beverage company finds the same corporate action praised in one region and boycotted in another, while local franchisees demand contradictory public statements and employees ask the company to take sides.

Develop a framework for how a global consumer brand should act and communicate when geopolitically driven consumer activism pulls its regional markets in opposing directions.
